title: Non-self-averaging topological Anderson insulator
abstract: Current research on the disordered topological quantum phases primarily focuses on the uncorrelated and short-range correlated disorder regime. These topological Anderson insulators are typically self-averaging. However, topological quantum systems with long-range correlated disorder have received limited attention due to the absence of tractable analytical methods. In fact, the long-range correlated disorder introduces more complex effects on topological quantum states. Here, we demonstrate that the long-range correlated disorder could induce anomalously statistical feature where the topological Anderson states become non-self-averaging, and the phase diagram is strongly dependent on individual disorder configurations. We term this statistical phase the non-self-averaging topological Anderson insulator. The non-self-averaging property is identified by the non-vanishing finite values of the relative variance of the Lyapunov exponent in the thermodynamic limit, alongside the non-Gaussian distributions of the Lyapunov exponent. Consequently, the topological properties of a single disordered sample deviate from the ensemble average, causing a breakdown of the central limit theorem. The non-self-averaging topological Anderson insulator provides insights into the interplay between correlated disorder and topology.
summary: This work explores how long-range correlated disorder fundamentally changes the nature of topological Anderson insulators, causing them to become non-self-averaging. The authors demonstrate this by showing that the relative variance of the Lyapunov exponent remains finite in the thermodynamic limit, indicating a breakdown of standard averaging theorems for these complex quantum states.
main_problem: The research investigates topological Anderson insulators under long-range correlated disorder, a regime poorly understood compared to standard uncorrelated disorder.
main_result: Long-range correlated disorder can induce non-self-averaging behavior in the topological states, meaning single sample properties deviate significantly from ensemble averages.
method: The analysis relies on calculating and analyzing the relative variance of the Lyapunov exponent ($\gamma$) across multiple disorder realizations to diagnose self-averaging versus non-self-averaging regimes.
model_or_system: The model used is a disordered Su-Schrieffer-Heeger (SSH) chain, incorporating long-range correlated disorder defined by a power-law spectral density $S(k) \sim 1/k^\alpha$.
key_observables: Topological Quantum Number ($Q$), Lyapunov Exponent ($\gamma$), and the Relative Variance of the Lyapunov Exponent ($R_\gamma$).
important_parameters: The correlation parameter $\alpha$ (quantifying disorder range), the system size $N$, and the number of disorder realizations $N_r$.
main_assumptions: Calculations are performed at half-filling using large system sizes ($N = 5 	imes 10^4$) and many disorder realizations ($N_r = 10^5$).
figures_summary: Figure 1 shows how $R_\gamma$ behaves for different $\alpha$, indicating non-self-averaging when $R_\gamma$ remains finite in the thermodynamic limit. Figure 2 plots average and relative variance of $\gamma$ vs. $N$, confirming fixed constant values for non-self-averaging cases.
paper_structure: The paper establishes the problem by contrasting self-averaging (short-range disorder) with the complex effects of long-range correlated disorder, demonstrating mathematically that this correlation leads to a finite relative variance in the thermodynamic limit, defining the 'non-self-averaging topological Anderson insulator'.
why_interesting: The breakdown of self-averaging is a critical concept in disordered systems theory, suggesting that standard ensemble averaging techniques fail to capture the true physics near topological phase transitions.
